items.new: Now, to anyone not fully acquainted with the ways of whales, it might seem an absurdly hopeless task to seek out one solitary creature in the boundless oceans of this planet. But not so to Ahab. He knew the patterns of all tides and currents. By calculating the drifting of the sperm whale's food, and by recalling the regular, established seasons for hunting him in particular latitudes, he could arrive at reasonable estimates — almost approaching certainty — about the most timely day to be on this or that ground in search of his prey.

items.new: So well established, in fact, is the sperm whale's periodic return to given waters that many hunters believe that, if he could be closely observed and studied throughout the world — if the logs for a single voyage of the entire whale fleet were carefully compared — then the migrations of the sperm whale would be found as unvarying as those of the herring shoals or the flights of swallows. On this hint, attempts have been made to construct elaborate migratory charts of the sperm whale.*

items.new: *Since the above was written, the statement is happily confirmed by an official circular issued by Lieutenant Maury, of the National Observatory, Washington, April 16th, 1851. By that circular, it appears that precisely such a chart is being completed, and portions of it are presented in the circular. "This chart divides the ocean into districts of five degrees of latitude by five degrees of longitude; perpendicularly through each of which districts are twelve columns for the twelve months; and horizontally through each district are three lines; one to show the number of days that have been spent in each month in every district, and the two others to show the number of days in which whales, sperm or right, have been seen."

items.new: But not only did each of these famous whales enjoy great individual celebrity — indeed, you may call it ocean-wide renown; not only was he famous in life and is now immortal in forecastle stories after death; but he was admitted into all the rights, privileges, and distinctions of a name, and had as much of a name, in fact, as Cambyses or Caesar. Was it not so, O Timor Tom! you famous leviathan, scarred like an iceberg, who lurked so long in the Oriental straits of that name, whose spout was often seen from the palmy beach of Ombay? Was it not so, O New Zealand Jack! you terror of all cruisers that crossed their wakes in the neighborhood of the Tattoo Land? Was it not so, O Morquan! King of Japan, whose lofty jet, they say, at times took on the likeness of a snow-white cross against the sky? Was it not so, O Don Miguel! you Chilian whale, marked like an old tortoise with mystic hieroglyphics upon your back! In plain prose, here are four whales as well known to students of Cetacean History as Marius or Sylla to the classical scholar.

But I have always found that when I have described to them some specific example of this twofold enormousness, they have pointedly complimented me on my facetiousness — when, I declare upon my soul, I was no more trying to be funny than Moses when he wrote the history of the plagues of Egypt.

items.new: First: In the year 1820 the ship Essex, Captain Pollard, of Nantucket, was cruising in the Pacific Ocean. One day she saw spouts, lowered her boats, and gave chase to a shoal of sperm whales. Before long several of the whales were wounded, when suddenly a very large whale, escaping from the boats, broke out of the shoal and bore straight down upon the ship. Dashing his forehead against her hull, he stove her in so badly that in less than "ten minutes" she settled down and fell over. Not a surviving plank of her has been seen since. After the most severe exposure, part of the crew reached land in their boats. When he had at last returned home, Captain Pollard sailed once more for the Pacific in command of another ship, but the gods shipwrecked him again on unknown rocks and breakers; for the second time his ship was utterly lost, and, at once forswearing the sea, he has never tempted it since. Captain Pollard lives in Nantucket to this day. I have seen Owen Chace, who was chief mate of the Essex at the time of the tragedy; I have read his plain and faithful narrative; I have talked with his son; and all this within a few miles of the scene of the catastrophe.*

items.new: *The following are extracts from Chace's narrative: "Every fact seemed to warrant me in concluding that it was anything but chance which directed his operations; he made two separate attacks upon the ship, at a short interval between them, both of which, according to their direction, were calculated to do us the most injury, by being made ahead, and thereby combining the speed of the two objects for the shock; to effect which, the exact maneuvers which he made were necessary. His aspect was most horrible, and such as indicated resentment and fury. He came directly from the shoal which we had just before entered, and in which we had struck three of his companions, as if fired with revenge for their sufferings." Again: "At all events, the whole circumstances taken together, all happening before my own eyes, and producing, at the time, impressions in my mind of decided, calculating mischief on the part of the whale (many of which impressions I cannot now recall), induce me to be satisfied that I am correct in my opinion."
